overview:
Preksha Meditation (Prekṣā-dhyāna) is a modern Jain contemplative system developed within the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth tradition under the guidance of Ācārya Tulsi (1914–1997) and systematized by Ācārya Mahāprajña (1920–2010). Although its formal structure is contemporary, its conceptual foundations draw on classical Jain teachings on perception (prekṣā), concentration (dhāraṇā), equanimity (samatā), and the purification of consciousness (citta-śuddhi). The term *prekṣā* means “to see carefully,” “to perceive distinctly,” or “to observe with full awareness.” In practice, it refers to a disciplined mode of inner observation that aims to cultivate non-reactive awareness of bodily sensations, breath, psychic centers, and mental states.

Preksha Meditation emerged in the mid-20th century as part of the Terāpanth movement’s efforts to articulate a structured, accessible path of spiritual development for laypeople while remaining grounded in Jain ethical and philosophical principles. Its curriculum includes several components: perception of breath (*śvāsa-prekṣā*), perception of body (*śarīra-prekṣā*), perception of psychic centers (*caitanya-kendra-prekṣā*), perception of colors (*leśyā-dhyāna*), and contemplative reflection (*anuprekṣā*). These practices are framed as methods to reduce the intensity of passions (*kaṣāyas*), weaken karmic influx (*āsrava*), and support the gradual movement toward equanimity.

Although widely taught in Terāpanth educational institutions, Preksha Meditation is not presented as a replacement for classical Jain soteriology. Instead, it is described as a practical method for cultivating mindfulness, ethical sensitivity, and emotional regulation within the constraints of modern life. Its promoters emphasize alignment with canonical Jain concepts such as *jñāna*, *darśana*, *cāritra*, and *tapas*, while acknowledging that the structured modules and terminology reflect contemporary pedagogical needs. Scholars note that Preksha Meditation represents one of the most influential modern Jain meditation systems, contributing to global interest in Jain approaches to nonviolence, self-awareness, and mental discipline.

Because Preksha Meditation is a modern system, its textual grounding relies on interpretive use of classical sources rather than direct canonical prescriptions. The following primary passages illustrate the conceptual foundations—perception, equanimity, and awareness—without implying that the canonical texts describe Preksha Meditation as a formal method.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha-sūtra 1.1. Preksha Meditation is framed by Terāpanth teachers as a practical aid for cultivating right conduct and reducing passions, aligning with the canonical emphasis on the three jewels.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.original_text: एवमेव अहं णिव्वुओ भावेणं भावं पेक्खामि
primary_sources.transliteration: evameva ahaṃ nivvuo bhāveṇaṃ bhāvaṃ pekkhāmi
primary_sources.translation: Thus, being detached, I observe the states of the mind with the mind.
primary_sources.notes: Ācārāṅga-sūtra I.6 (Prakrit). This passage is often cited to illustrate the ancient Jain emphasis on mindful observation (*pekkhā*), which Preksha Meditation adapts into a structured modern practice.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Śvetāmbara tradition
primary_sources.original_text: संतो धम्मं पेक्खन्तो, णिव्वुओ भावेण भावं
primary_sources.transliteration: saṃto dhammaṃ pekkhanto, nivvuo bhāveṇa bhāvaṃ
primary_sources.translation: The wise perceive the dharma, observing mental states with detachment.
primary_sources.notes: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra 29.72. Used in Terāpanth commentaries to support the idea that careful perception is a classical Jain contemplative method.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
primary_sources.author: Early Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.translation: Through meditation, one perceives the dharma.
primary_sources.notes: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2. This verse is cited in modern Jain meditation literature to show that perception and meditation are linked in early texts.

misconceptions.myth: Preksha Meditation is an ancient Jain practice taught exactly in its current form by Mahāvīra.
misconceptions.reality: While rooted in classical Jain concepts of perception and equanimity, Preksha Meditation is a modern system developed in the 20th century by Terāpanth leaders. The canonical texts do not describe its structured modules.

misconceptions.myth: Preksha Meditation replaces traditional Jain vows and ethical disciplines.
misconceptions.reality: Terāpanth teachers consistently state that Preksha Meditation complements, rather than replaces, the foundational Jain path of vows, ethical conduct, and scriptural study.

misconceptions.myth: Preksha Meditation is identical to Buddhist mindfulness or modern secular meditation.
misconceptions.reality: Although sharing some phenomenological similarities, Preksha Meditation is explicitly grounded in Jain metaphysics, karma theory, and the cultivation of nonviolence, making its aims and interpretive framework distinct.
